story: Matsya, the fish form of the god Vishnu, is described as rescuing the first man, Manu, from a great flood. In the earliest account, Manu, performing a ritual, finds a tiny fish in his hands. The fish says it fears being eaten by larger fish and asks for protection, promising in return to save Manu from a coming flood. Manu agrees, placing the fish first in a pot, then in a larger ditch, and finally, once it has grown large enough, releasing it into the ocean. The fish thanks him, warns him of the exact day of the flood, and tells him to build a boat that can be tied to its horn. When the flood arrives, Manu ties his boat to the fish's horn, and the fish tows the boat through the storm to the high ground of the Himalayas, saving him. Afterward, Manu performs sacrifices, and from these the goddess Ida appears; together they produce a new race of humans. In later versions, the fish reveals itself to be Brahma, and grants Manu creative power. Other tellings add that Manu gathers seven sages, plant seeds, and pairs of animals into the boat before the flood, preserving them all. In another cycle of stories, a demon named Hayagriva steals the sacred Vedas from a sleeping Brahma. Vishnu descends to earth as a small fish, is found and nurtured by a king named Satyavrata in the same growing manner, reveals its identity, warns of a flood, and after guiding the king's boat to safety, kills the demon and returns the stolen scriptures to Brahma. Satyavrata is then made Vaivasvata Manu, ruler of the current age of humanity.
